generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

Suppose we want to evaluate \( \displaystyle \int \int _D {@quest_expr@} \,dA\)

where \(D\) is the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) quadrant in between \({@eq_circle_1@}\) and \({@eq_circle_2@}\)

We can follow this approach


Since \(D\) is a portion of a ring, we can determine the integral using polar coordinates.


Step 1: We need to set up the limits of integration from the sketch above.

The limits of the angle are \(\pi \leq \theta \leq \frac{3}{2}\pi\)

The limits of the radius are \(1 \leq r \leq 3\)


Step 2: The next thing is to convert the function into polar form.

Recall that, \(y={@y@}\) and \(x={@x@}\) and \(\,dA= r \cdot \,dr \,d\theta\)

Therefore, in polar coordinates, \({@quest_expr@} = {@ta5@} \quad (\text{eqn}1)\)


Step 3: Compute the area of the bounded region as follows.

\( \begin{align*} \displaystyle \int \int _D {@quest_expr@} \,dA &= \int_ {\theta_1}^ {\theta_2} \int_{r_1}^{r_2} (r^2 \sin^2(\theta) + {@coeff_3@} r \cos(\theta)) r \,dr \,d\theta \\ &= \int_ {\pi}^ {\frac{3}{2}\pi} \int_{1}^{3} r^3 \sin^2(\theta) + {@coeff_3@} r^2 \cos(\theta) \,dr \,d\theta \\ &= \int_ {\pi}^ {\frac{3}{2}\pi} \left[ \frac{r^4}{4} \sin^2(\theta) + {@coeff_3/3@} r^3 \cos(\theta) \right]^{r=3} _{r=1} \,d\theta \\ &= \int_ {\pi}^ {\frac{3}{2}\pi} 20 \sin^2(\theta) + {@coeff_3*26/3@} \cos(\theta) \,d\theta \\ &= \int_ {\pi}^ {\frac{3}{2}\pi} 10 - 10 \cos(2\theta) + {@coeff_3*26/3@} \cos(\theta) \,d\theta \quad \text{since} \quad \sin^2(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} (1 - \cos(2\theta)) \\ &= \left[ 10\theta - 5 \sin(2\theta) + {@coeff_3*26/3@} \sin(\theta) \right]^{\frac{3}{2}\pi} _{\pi} \\ &= 5\pi - {@coeff_3*26/3@} \\ &= {@theta_integration@} \quad \text{(2dp)} \end{align*} \)
